name: Conformally Dressed Black Hole in Three Dimensions
description: A static, circularly symmetric black hole of three dimensions with a negative cosmological constant, surrounded by a massless, conformally coupled scalar field that is finite on its horizon and everywhere outside it, found by Cristián Martínez and Jorge Zanelli in 1996. The curvature diverges at its centre, the entropy is two thirds of a quarter of the length of its horizon, and it is unstable to circularly symmetric perturbations.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit, with $l$ the anti-de Sitter radius and $B \geq 0$ the one constant of the solution, which puts the horizon at $r = 2B$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: "The scalar field is regular everywhere," Cristián Martínez and Jorge Zanelli wrote of the black hole of three dimensions they found in 1996 at the Centro de Estudios Científicos de Santiago [martinez1996]. They added the field to gravity with the cosmological constant $-1/l^2$, the theory in which Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Zanelli had found in 1992 the black hole named BTZ after them [banados1992, martinez1996]. The field $\Psi$ has no mass, and a term $-\tfrac{1}{16}R\Psi^2$ in the action couples it to the curvature so that its action is unchanged when the metric and the field are rescaled together [martinez1996]. With the time chosen so that $g_{tt}g_{rr} = -1$, they found $g^{rr} = (r + B)^2(r - 2B)/(rl^2)$ and $\Psi = \sqrt{8B/(\kappa(r + B))}$, where $\kappa$ is the gravitational constant and $B \geq 0$ the one constant of the solution [martinez1996]. With the same coupling in four dimensions and no cosmological constant, the black hole is the one named after N. M. Bocharova, K. A. Bronnikov, V. N. Melnikov, and Jacob D. Bekenstein, whose metric is the extreme Reissner-Nordström one and whose field is unbounded at the horizon [martinez1996]. Martínez and Zanelli found the cosmological constant necessary for their black hole [martinez1996].¶The stress tensor of a conformally coupled field has no trace, so the Ricci scalar is $-6/l^2$ at every point, as in anti-de Sitter space [martinez1996]. The horizon is the null circle $r = 2B$, and the Kretschmann scalar, $12(r^6 + 2B^6)/(l^4r^6)$, diverges only at $r = 0$, inside it [martinez1996]. Far away the metric approaches anti-de Sitter space with no term linear in $r$, so its asymptotic symmetries form the conformal group of two dimensions, as for pure gravity [martinez1996, natsuume2000a]. Makoto Natsuume, Takashi Okamura, and Masamichi Sato showed in 2000 that the Cotton tensor, which vanishes for a conformally flat metric in three dimensions, vanishes for this one only far away, so the black hole is not locally anti-de Sitter space [natsuume2000a]. The field reaches $\sqrt{8/\kappa}$ at $r = 0$ and falls off as $r^{-1/2}$ far away [martinez1996, henneaux2002]. One constant fixes both the mass and the field, which has no conserved charge of its own, so that in the words of Martínez and Zanelli it "produces no new hair" [martinez1996].¶Requiring the Euclidean geometry to be regular at the horizon, Martínez and Zanelli found the temperature $9r_+/(16\pi l^2)$, with $r_+ = 2B$ [martinez1996]. From the Euclidean action, in units with $\kappa = 8\pi$, they found the mass $3r_+^2/(32l^2)$ and the entropy $\pi r_+/3$, which together satisfy the first law [martinez1996]. That entropy is two thirds of $\pi r_+/2$, a quarter of the length of the horizon [martinez1996]. Natsuume, Okamura, and Sato traced the factor to the coupling, which scales the gravitational constant at the horizon by a factor that depends on $\Psi$, and in the conformally related Einstein metric the entropy obeys the area law [natsuume2000a]. Counting the states of a conformal field theory on the boundary with the central charge of pure gravity, they found an entropy with the same dependence on the mass and a larger coefficient, equal to that of the BTZ hole of the same mass [natsuume2000a]. Kun Meng, Zhan-Ning Hu, and Liu Zhao counted states with a conformal symmetry near the horizon in 2014, found a central charge that depends on the field there, and recovered the factor of two thirds [meng2014].¶In a note added to their article, Martínez and Zanelli pointed to a family of black holes with a scalar field that Kevin C. K. Chan, at the University of Waterloo, had posted two and a half weeks earlier, and called the connection "not completely clear to these authors at the moment" [martinez1996, chan1997]. Chan showed in his revised version of January 1997 that a member of his family, rewritten with the field $\Psi$, is their black hole [chan1997]. Natsuume and Okamura set the hole rotating in 2000 by mixing its time and angle, the change that turns the static BTZ hole into the rotating one, and the inner horizon of the rotating hole is a curvature singularity [natsuume2000b]. At the extreme value $|J| = Ml$ of its angular momentum $J$ and mass $M$, the singularity disappears and the solution becomes the extreme BTZ hole [natsuume2000b]. Eloy Ayón-Beato, Alberto García, Alfredo Macías, and José M. Pérez-Sánchez showed in 2000 that, among static, circularly symmetric metrics with $g_{tt}g_{rr} = -1$ and any coupling $\zeta R\Psi^2$, this black hole at $\zeta = 1/8$ is the only solution that is not locally anti-de Sitter space [ayonbeato2000scalar]. At the same coupling they found a field $\Psi \propto r^{-1/2}$ on anti-de Sitter space whose stress tensor vanishes [ayonbeato2000scalar].¶Martínez and Zanelli computed in 1997 the back reaction of a quantum conformal field on the static BTZ hole, and found the corrected metric of the same form as their black hole [martinez1997]. The stress tensor stays traceless at one loop in three dimensions, so the classical and the semiclassical equations have the same solutions, with the constants of integration fixed in the classical one [martinez1997]. Martínez proved in 1998 that the black hole is unstable, with circularly symmetric perturbations of the field and the metric that grow as $e^{\sigma t}$ for $\sigma > 9r_+/(2l^2)$ [martinez1998]. Marc Henneaux, Martínez, Ricardo Troncoso, and Zanelli rescaled the metric in 2002 to make the field minimally coupled, a field $\phi$ with the potential $-\cosh^6\phi/(8l^2)$, and in that frame the entropy is a quarter of the length of the horizon [henneaux2002]. The field falls off so slowly that it adds to the conserved charges, and they found the asymptotic symmetries and the central charge of pure gravity unchanged [henneaux2002]. Jack Gegenberg, Martínez, and Troncoso found in 2003 that a black hole of the family Henneaux and coauthors found in that frame, of which this one is a member, can decay in a heat bath into the BTZ hole of the same temperature [gegenberg2003].¶Marcela Cárdenas, Oscar Fuentealba, and Martínez found in 2014 that the same metric holds an electric field as well, when that field obeys the conformally invariant Lagrangian $(-F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})^{3/4}$ and the scalar field is larger by a factor $\sqrt{a}$ with $a > 1$ [cardenas2014]. Luis Avilés, Hideki Maeda, and Martínez found in 2018 a solution in which a conformally coupled scalar field collapses from regular initial data in the massless BTZ spacetime and, for some values of its parameters, settles in the far future to this static black hole [aviles2018]. They noted that the black hole could then be stable beyond linear order, or that the growing modes Martínez found are absent from their solution or obey other conditions at infinity [aviles2018].

related.text: The black hole of the same theory with no field, whose curvature is constant. At $B = 0$ this metric is the BTZ hole of zero mass, and at a given mass the two holes are different solutions [henneaux2002].

The BTZ hole with the backreaction of strongly coupled quantum fields, whose metric gains a term in $1/r$. Martínez and Zanelli found a term of that form for a quantum conformal field at one loop, the form of this black hole's metric [martinez1997].

The vacuum of three dimensions with a negative cosmological constant, which this black hole approaches far from its horizon. Nearer in, its Cotton tensor is not zero, so it is not locally anti-de Sitter space [natsuume2000a].

Schwarzschild's hole in four dimensions with a minimally coupled scalar field that grows along an axis and is smooth on the horizon. Here the field is coupled to the curvature and falls off far away, and the hole needs the negative cosmological constant [martinez1996].

Friedmann universes of dust whose particles interact with a conformally coupled scalar field in four dimensions. The coupling constant of the field to the curvature is $1/6$ there and $1/8$ in three dimensions, the values that keep the action of the field unchanged when the metric and the field are rescaled together [martinez1996].

Light falling in from the boundary of anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions and leaving a BTZ hole. Avilés, Maeda, and Martínez worked through it before following a conformally coupled scalar field that collapses to a black hole [aviles2018].

A point charge with Maxwell's field in three dimensions, whose field falls off so slowly that it curves spacetime at every radius. Cárdenas, Fuentealba, and Martínez charged this black hole with Maxwell's Lagrangian raised to the power $3/4$, which is conformally invariant in three dimensions [cardenas2014].

coordinates.name: Static

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/l^2$
A length, $B \geq 0$, the one constant of the solution; the horizon is the circle $r = 2B$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta)$, where $t$ has dimensions of time. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r + B\right)^3\left(r - 2B\right)\left(r^2 - B\,r + B^2\right)}{l^4\,r^3}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r^2 - B\,r + B^2}{r\left(r + B\right)\left(r - 2B\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{\left(r + B\right)^2\left(r - 2B\right)}{l^2}\dot{\theta}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = -1/l^2$
A length, $B \geq 0$, the one constant of the solution; the horizon is the circle $r = 2B$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta)$, where the advanced time $v$ has dimensions of time, $c\,dv = c\,dt + rl^2\,dr/((r + B)^2(r - 2B))$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, so $\dot{v}$ in the geodesic equations means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\left(r + B\right)^3\left(r - 2B\right)\left(r^2 - B\,r + B^2\right)}{l^4\,r^3}\dot{v}^2 - \dfrac{2\left(r + B\right)\left(r^2 - B\,r + B^2\right)}{l^2\,r^2}\dot{v}\dot{r} - \dfrac{\left(r + B\right)^2\left(r - 2B\right)}{l^2}\dot{\theta}^2 = 0
